obj_pipeline v6.3.9 · MRO / HiRISE

HiRISE Pipeline Anatomy

Author Raymundo "R@y" Olguin HiRISE Operations Center (HiROC), Lunar and Planetary Laboratory, University of Arizona

The pipeline turns a HiRISE stereo Digital Terrain Model (DTM) into a true-scale, textured 3D terrain mesh, then measures the terrain and writes a science report. Everything runs locally in Python: GDAL reads the georeferenced rasters, NumPy builds the mesh, and five writers serialize it for desktop 3D tools, game engines and Apple Vision Pro.

Each section below is a working instrument: typeset equations you can copy as LaTeX, MATLAB-style plots, a 3D terrain surface, diagrams, and five simulations (run playback, hillshade lighting, ortho stretch, stereo geometry, Mars orbit). Python and MATLAB code sit side by side for the core algorithms. Example numbers are marked as examples; everything else is taken directly from the code.

6processing stages per project
5mesh formats: OBJ, PLY, FBX, GLB, USDZ
3report formats: HTML, PDF, LaTeX
6code layers, imports flow one way
~26.5klines of Python in 30 modules

    03 · Setup

    Install on another computer

    Copy the HiRISE_Pipeline folder and double-click SETUP.bat. It installs Miniforge when it is missing and builds the environment from the lock file. The lock fixes every package to an exact file and checksum, so each computer ends up with the same versions you tested.

    0things to install by hand: SETUP.bat installs Miniforge (free, no admin rights) when it is missing
    117packages in the Windows lock, all pinned
    3.12.15Python version
    3.13.3GDAL + JP2 plugin
    1×internet needed, only while setting up

    04 · How it works

    Pipeline flow

    One command starts the run. The pipeline loads the optional emission-angle manifest once, finds every project folder, then runs the same six stages on each project. Select a step to see the functions it calls, the variables it produces and their units.

    Stage 0, GeoTIFF extraction (v6.3.0). When a project's DTM is a PDS .IMG, the pipeline first converts every DTM .IMG to GeoTIF/<same name>.TIF with the rules of R@y's standalone converter v8: the detached .LBL is opened when present, the GeoTIFF is tiled, DEFLATE, predictor 3 and BigTIFF, and elevations, georeferencing and NoData are copied unchanged. Files already converted are skipped, writes are atomic, and the rest of the run reads the DTM from the GeoTIFF. --geotiff-only (or RUN.bat mode 4) runs just this converter for a whole dataset, with the COMPLETE / PARTIAL / EMPTY report and cleanup of empty GeoTIF/ folders.

    05 · Software architecture

    Front end and back end

    Since the web app was removed there is no server and no database. The "front end" is two things a person actually sees: the terminal interface that collects the run settings, and the HTML report that presents the results in a browser. The "back end" is the obj_pipeline Python package, and the data layer is the file system.

    Front end · input

    Terminal UI

    • RUN.bat: Windows batch wizard, 5 steps, finds a Python that can import GDAL
    • cli.py: argparse flags plus the two box-drawn menus (format, ortho encoding)
    • Validates paths, rejects search-ms: and URI pastes
    Back end · compute

    obj_pipeline

    • Pure Python 3.12 package, no network calls
    • GDAL / OSR for raster and CRS work, NumPy for arrays
    • Single process, one project at a time, memory fallback doubles the downsample on MemoryError
    Front end · output

    Reports + meshes

    • HTML report: Python writes the data into the page, the browser draws it with Plotly, ECharts and D3
    • PDF (ReportLab) and LaTeX source
    • Mesh files opened in Blender, Twinmotion, Unity, Vision Pro

    07 · Geospatial data pipeline

    From pixels to Mars coordinates

    A DTM is a grid of elevation posts. On its own a grid has no location; two pieces of metadata stored in the GeoTIFF put it on Mars. The GeoTransform maps a pixel (column, row) to projected map coordinates in metres. The projection (a WKT string, usually equirectangular or polar stereographic on the Mars 2000 sphere) defines how those metres relate to longitude and latitude.

    \begin{aligned} X_{\text{map}} &= g_0 + g_1\left(c+\tfrac{1}{2}\right) + g_2\left(r+\tfrac{1}{2}\right) \quad [\mathrm{m}]\\ Y_{\text{map}} &= g_3 + g_4\left(c+\tfrac{1}{2}\right) + g_5\left(r+\tfrac{1}{2}\right) \quad [\mathrm{m}] \end{aligned}
    \lambda = \lambda_0 + \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\,\frac{X_{\text{map}}}{R\cos\varphi_1},\qquad \varphi = \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\,\frac{Y_{\text{map}}}{R},\qquad R = 3\,396\,190\ \mathrm{m}
    \Delta x = \sqrt{g_1^2 + g_2^2},\quad \Delta y = \sqrt{g_4^2 + g_5^2},\qquad \lambda' = \begin{cases}\lambda - 360^\circ & \lambda > 180^\circ\\ \lambda & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
    Fig. 2c · Geospatial transform chainwhat happens to one DTM post
    Pixel to longitude / latitude 
    # ingest/coordinates.py (condensed)
ds  = gdal.Open(str(dtm_path))
gt  = ds.GetGeoTransform()
cx  = gt[0] + gt[1]*ds.RasterXSize/2 + gt[2]*ds.RasterYSize/2
cy  = gt[3] + gt[4]*ds.RasterXSize/2 + gt[5]*ds.RasterYSize/2
src = osr.SpatialReference(); src.ImportFromWkt(ds.GetProjection())
src.SetAxisMappingStrategy(osr.OAMS_TRADITIONAL_GIS_ORDER)
geo = src.CloneGeogCS()                       # keeps the Mars datum
geo.SetAxisMappingStrategy(osr.OAMS_TRADITIONAL_GIS_ORDER)
lon, lat, _ = osr.CoordinateTransformation(src, geo).TransformPoint(cx, cy)
if lon > 180: lon -= 360
    % MATLAB (Mapping Toolbox) equivalent
[Z, R] = readgeoraster('DTEEC_082989_1630_083055_1630_A01.TIF');
[xc, yc] = intrinsicToWorld(R, R.RasterSize(2)/2 + 0.5, R.RasterSize(1)/2 + 0.5);
p = R.ProjectedCRS;                           % from the GeoTIFF WKT
[lat, lon] = projinv(p, xc, yc);              % degrees on the Mars datum
if lon > 180, lon = lon - 360; end
    Fig. 2 · GeoTransform explorerexample values · Mars sphere R = 3,396,190 m

    Longitude / latitude here use the equirectangular inverse on a sphere (λ = X / R, φ = Y / R, centre longitude 0, standard parallel 0) so you can see the relationship. The pipeline itself never hard-codes a projection: it reads the WKT and lets osr.CoordinateTransformation do the inverse for whatever projection the DTM uses.

    Coordinate extraction, in order of trust

    PrioritySourceHow
    1DTM rastergdal.Open → GeoTransform → centre pixel → osr.SpatialReference.ImportFromWkt → CloneGeogCS() (keeps the Mars datum) → CoordinateTransformation.TransformPoint for the centre and four corners (bounding box in degrees)
    2Selected ORTHO JP2Same procedure on the ortho if the DTM has no usable CRS
    3gdalinfo -jsonLast-resort metadata scrape through a subprocess
    refFolder name labelOnly for comparison. 3087E_425N means 308.7° E, 42.5° N (tenths of a degree). The report shows the difference |GDAL − folder|.
    Fig. 3 · Folder label parseringest/coordinates.py · parse_folder_coordinate_label()

    Regex (\d{2,5})([EW])[_\- ]?(\d{2,5})([NS]). W and S become negative. Mars longitudes are usually east-positive 0 to 360°, so anything above 180° has 360° subtracted to match GDAL's −180 to +180 output.

    Details that keep the numbers right

    • Axis order. GDAL 3 is axis-order aware. Both CRSs are set to OAMS_TRADITIONAL_GIS_ORDER so every transform returns (longitude, latitude), never (latitude, longitude).
    • Planet detection. _detect_body_name looks for "mars" in the CRS text, or a semi-major axis within 20 km of 3,396,190 m (Mars), 1,737,400 m (Moon) or 6,378,137 m (Earth).
    • NoData. Pixels outside the GDAL mask band, equal to the NoData value, or with |z| > 1030 become NaN and never become vertices.
    • Data paths. core/gdal_env.py sets PROJ_DATA and GDAL_DATA from the running Python's folders when they are not already set, so projection lookups work without conda activate.

    How DATA/ stays connected (v5.8.3)

    Every spreadsheet row that describes location reads from one helper, _geo() in reports/data_export.py. It takes the GeoTransform and CRS that GDAL read in Stage 1, so the same parameter can never show two different values in two workbooks. tools/audit_data_export.py reopens the DTM, recomputes each value independently and fails the build if any cell disagrees.

    ParameterComputed fromWhere it appears
    GeoTransform g0 to g5GDAL GetGeoTransform(), g5 kept signedRASTER_PARAMETERS, DTM_KPI G17
    Bounds (m and deg)4 corners through the GeoTransform, then OSRSPATIAL_EXTENTS (West, East, South, North bound), CRS sheet, DTM_KPI G11/G12
    DTM centre lon/latGeoTransform at (W/2, H/2), OSR into CloneGeogCS(), lon in −180..180 and 0–360 ECRS sheet, SPATIAL_EXTENTS, STEREO_PAIR, GEOLOGICAL_CONTEXT, EDL, MISSION, ACQUISITION, DTM_KPI G04/G05/G10
    Central meridian, latitude of originProjection parameters of the WKT (constants, not the site)CRS sheet and DTM_KPI G13 to G15, labelled as projection parameters
    Mesh originbuild_mesh: midpoint of the vertex X and Y rangeMESH_STATISTICS, XR sheet, SPATIAL_EXTENTS, DTM_KPI M11/M12
    MESH_VERTICESSame rows, columns and NoData mask as the mesh; pixel centres; batch OSRPOINTCLOUD/MESH_VERTICES.csv and .xlsx (id, row, col, lon, lat, lon 0–360, elev, x/y proj, x/y mesh)
    Feature distancesGreat-circle distance (haversine form) on the Mars sphere from the DTM centreMARS_GLOBAL_CONTEXT
    x_{\text{mesh}} = X_{\text{map}} - X_0,\qquad y_{\text{mesh}} = Y_{\text{map}} - Y_0,\qquad X_0 = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\min X + \max X\right),\; Y_0 = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\min Y + \max Y\right)
    d = 2R\,\arcsin\sqrt{\sin^2\tfrac{\varphi_2-\varphi_1}{2} + \cos\varphi_1\cos\varphi_2\,\sin^2\tfrac{\lambda_2-\lambda_1}{2}},\qquad R = 3\,396\,190\ \mathrm{m}

    Audit result on an equirectangular DTM (−16.96° N, 8.66° E) and a north polar stereographic DTM (84.34° N, 26.57° E): 18 of 18 geospatial checks pass and 536 of 536 rows are filled in each. In v5.8.2 the same audit failed 15 checks per project. Mesh files stayed byte-identical.

    08 · Math modeling

    Mesh math

    The mesh is a regular grid: one vertex per sampled DTM post, one quad per square of four valid posts. All of it is vectorized NumPy with no Python loops over samples (geometry/terrain.py).

    1 · Choosing the downsample

    # compute_downsample(height, width, requested, budget) T_full = 2·(H − 1)·(W − 1) # triangles at native posting s = 1 if T_full ≤ B # B = --tri-budget, default 10,000,000 s = ⌈ √(T_full / B) ⌉ otherwise # or the user's --downsample while T(s) > B: s ← s + 1 # exact count incl. the kept last row/col (v5.9.0) # the last row and column are always appended so the mesh reaches the raster edge
    Fig. 4 · Decimation on a synthetic DTM64 × 40 posts · colour = elevation (report colour ramp)

    Dots are the posts that become vertices. Vertex count falls as roughly 1/s², and the effective post spacing becomes s × the native spacing.

    Fig. 5 · Downsample calculator for a real DTMsame formula as compute_downsample()

    Example dimensions only. A 1 m HiRISE DTM is typically a few thousand posts wide and tens of thousands tall.

    2 · Vertices, UVs and centring

    x = gt0 + gt1·(c + 0.5) + gt2·(r + 0.5) # metres, easting y = gt3 + gt4·(c + 0.5) + gt5·(r + 0.5) # metres, northing z = elevation[r, c] · vert_exag # metres; RUN.bat always passes 1.0 (no exaggeration) x ← x − (min x + max x)/2 # centre X and Y on the origin y ← y − (min y + max y)/2 # Z stays absolute (areoid-referenced elevation) (col, row) = G_ortho⁻¹ (x, y) # vertex position in the ORTHO's own pixel grid (v5.9.0) u = col / W_ortho, v = 1 − row / H_ortho # pixel edges on integers; exact for any ortho footprint # no georeferenced ortho: u = (c + ½)/W, v = 1 − (r + ½)/H on the DTM grid # GLB only: v_glTF = 1 − v (glTF puts the UV origin at the image's top-left)

    3 · Faces and normals

    # one quad per grid square, kept only if all four corners are valid (finite) quad = (i00, i10, i11, i01) triangles = (a, b, c) and (a, c, d) # same winding in every exporter n_face = (p1 − p0) × (p2 − p0) # cross product; length = 2 × triangle area n_vert = normalize( Σ n_face over touching faces ) # area-weighted, via np.bincount scatter if mean(n_z) < 0: n ← −n # make normals point up (+Z)

    The vertex index map idx starts as −1 everywhere and gets consecutive numbers only where the sample is finite, so NoData holes become real holes in the mesh instead of spikes. If NumPy runs out of memory, process_project retries with the downsample doubled, up to 64×.

    Typeset model

    T_{\text{full}} = 2\,(H-1)(W-1),\qquad s = \min\left\{ s' \ge \left\lceil \sqrt{T_{\text{full}}/B}\,\right\rceil : T(s') \le B \right\},\quad T(s) = 2\,(n_r(s)-1)(n_c(s)-1),\qquad B = 10^{7}
    \mathbf{v}_{rc} = \begin{pmatrix} g_0 + g_1(c+\frac12) + g_2(r+\frac12) - \bar{x} \\ g_3 + g_4(c+\frac12) + g_5(r+\frac12) - \bar{y} \\ k_{\text{VE}}\, z_{rc} \end{pmatrix},\quad \bar{x} = \tfrac12(\min x + \max x),\quad \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{col} \\ \mathrm{row} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} o_1 & o_2 \\ o_4 & o_5 \end{pmatrix}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} x - o_0 \\ y - o_3 \end{pmatrix},\quad (u, v) = \left(\frac{\mathrm{col}}{W_o},\; 1 - \frac{\mathrm{row}}{H_o}\right)
    \mathbf{n}_f = (\mathbf{p}_1-\mathbf{p}_0)\times(\mathbf{p}_2-\mathbf{p}_0),\qquad \mathbf{n}_v = \frac{\sum_{f \ni v}\mathbf{n}_f}{\left\lVert \sum_{f \ni v}\mathbf{n}_f \right\rVert},\qquad \overline{n_z} < 0 \Rightarrow \mathbf{n} \leftarrow -\mathbf{n}

    Sim. 2 · Sun-angle hillshadelighting model for terrain shading · synthetic DTM
    \mathrm{HS} = 255\left[\cos Z\cos S + \sin Z \sin S \cos(A - \alpha)\right]

    Defaults are the report's fallback sun (azimuth 156.2°, elevation 26.4°). HiRISE images are taken mid-afternoon, so the sun sits low and relief casts long shading; elevation = 90° − incidence angle from the label.

    Mesh synthesis 
    # geometry/terrain.py · build_mesh() (condensed)
rows = np.arange(0, H, s); cols = np.arange(0, W, s)
if rows[-1] != H-1: rows = np.append(rows, H-1)
if cols[-1] != W-1: cols = np.append(cols, W-1)
z     = elevation[np.ix_(rows, cols)]
valid = np.isfinite(z)
cc, rr = np.meshgrid(cols + 0.5, rows + 0.5)
x = gt[0] + gt[1]*cc + gt[2]*rr
y = gt[3] + gt[4]*cc + gt[5]*rr
idx = np.full(z.shape, -1); idx[valid] = np.arange(valid.sum())
v = np.column_stack([x[valid], y[valid], z[valid]*vert_exag])
v[:, :2] -= (v[:, :2].min(0) + v[:, :2].max(0)) / 2
det = o[1]*o[5] - o[2]*o[4]                       # o = ortho GeoTransform
col = ( o[5]*(x-o[0]) - o[2]*(y-o[3])) / det
row = (-o[4]*(x-o[0]) + o[1]*(y-o[3])) / det
uv  = np.column_stack([col[valid]/Wo, 1 - row[valid]/Ho])
i00, i10, i11, i01 = idx[:-1,:-1], idx[1:,:-1], idx[1:,1:], idx[:-1,1:]
keep  = (i00>=0)&(i10>=0)&(i11>=0)&(i01>=0)
quads = np.column_stack([i00[keep], i10[keep], i11[keep], i01[keep]])
# normals: np.cross per triangle, np.bincount scatter to vertices, normalise
    % MATLAB equivalent (base MATLAB + Mapping Toolbox for readgeoraster)
[Z, R] = readgeoraster('dtm.tif', 'OutputType', 'double');
Z(abs(Z) > 1e30) = NaN;
[H, W] = size(Z);
Tfull = 2*(H-1)*(W-1);  B = 1e7;
if Tfull <= B, s = 1; else, s = ceil(sqrt(Tfull/B)); end
rows = 1:s:H; if rows(end) ~= H, rows(end+1) = H; end
cols = 1:s:W; if cols(end) ~= W, cols(end+1) = W; end
z = Z(rows, cols);  valid = isfinite(z);
[C, Rr] = meshgrid(cols, rows);
[x, y]  = intrinsicToWorld(R, C, Rr);          % pixel centres, metres
idx = zeros(size(z)); idx(valid) = 1:nnz(valid);   % 0 = invalid (1-based)
V = [x(valid), y(valid), z(valid)];
V(:,1:2) = V(:,1:2) - (min(V(:,1:2)) + max(V(:,1:2)))/2;
[oc, orr] = worldToIntrinsic(Ro, x, y);          % ortho pixel coords (centres on integers)
UV = [(oc(valid)-0.5)/Wo, 1-(orr(valid)-0.5)/Ho];
a = idx(1:end-1,1:end-1); b = idx(2:end,1:end-1);
c = idx(2:end,2:end);     d = idx(1:end-1,2:end);
k = a>0 & b>0 & c>0 & d>0;
T = [a(k) b(k) c(k); a(k) c(k) d(k)];           % triangles
Fn = cross(V(T(:,2),:)-V(T(:,1),:), V(T(:,3),:)-V(T(:,1),:), 2);
N  = zeros(size(V));
for j = 1:3
  N(:,j) = accumarray(T(:), repmat(Fn(:,j),3,1), [size(V,1) 1]);
end
N = N ./ max(vecnorm(N,2,2), eps);
if mean(N(:,3)) < 0, N = -N; end
trisurf(T, V(:,1), V(:,2), V(:,3), 'EdgeColor', 'none'); axis equal; camlight
    09 · Algorithm

    Ortho selection

    A HiRISE DTM folder usually holds several orthorectified images (orthos) from the two stereo observations: each image at its full resolution and as a reduced 1 m copy, sometimes colour products too. Since v6.2.0 the texture is chosen by a seven-step scientific method (ingest/ortho_science.py): the ortho that puts the most real detail in the right place on the terrain, and never one with holes when a complete one exists. Edit the example candidates below and run the selection; the log mimics the real terminal output. A separate page, HiRISE Ortho Selection (docs/HiRISE_Ortho_Selection.html), explains the method in full with a two-image calculator.

    Fig. 6 · Selection simulatorexample candidates · ingest/ortho_selection.py
    JP2 filebandgridbinningemission e (°)DTM coverage %jitterresult

    The method, as implemented

    Each step only narrows what the previous one kept; the order encodes the priorities.

    1. Inventory. Observation ID, colour band and grid letter from the file name (A = 0.25 m, B = 0.5 m, C = 1.0 m); EMISSION_ANGLE, INCIDENCE_ANGLE, MRO:BINNING and MAP_SCALE from the labels; the DTM's vertical RMS error Δz from the README.
    2. Eligibility. RED orthos only (colour products such as IRB are never the texture); unreadable or blank files rejected (≥ 90 % zero or NoData, or mean below 2 / 255).
    3. Native sampling. Per image, only the ortho at its real pixel size counts: bin 1 → A, bin 2 → B, bin 4 → C (McEwen et al. 2007). A finer grid is interpolated and dropped; a coarser grid is a backup. Without binning in a label, the finest grid HiROC produced for that image is native.
    4. Coverage of the DTM. Valid DTM posts where the ortho has real pixels ÷ all valid DTM posts, sampled at the DTM's own posts so the black frame around the strip does not count. More than 1 percentage point below the most complete candidate = backup: a hole is a total loss.
    5. Geometric fidelity. Images flagged for spacecraft jitter (--jitter-obs or JITTER.txt) are used only if nothing else is left (Sutton et al. 2017). The DTM height error shifts the draped image by Δz · tan e (Kirk et al. 2008).
    6. Score. E = √(g² + (Δz · tan e)²); the smallest wins. Without a README value Δz is 0.3 m for 1 m DTMs and 1.0 m for 2 m DTMs (Sutton et al. 2022), marked as assumed.
    7. Tie-break and record. Within 5 % of the best E: lower emission, then fewer saturated pixels, then higher coverage. If the winner fails to convert, the next in rank is used. Everything is written to JP2_CONVERTED/ORTHO_SELECTION.csv.
    Fig. 6b · Decision flowchartselect_best_jp2_ortho() · ortho_science.py
    flowchart TD
  A[Scan project for *.JP2, read labels and README] --> B{RED band and readable?}
  B -- no --> X1[reject]
  B -- yes --> C{grid matches the image's binning?}
  C -- finer --> X2[reject: interpolated]
  C -- coarser --> K[backup]
  C -- native --> D{coverage within 1 point of the best?}
  D -- no --> K
  D -- yes --> J{flagged for jitter and a clean one exists?}
  J -- yes --> K
  J -- no --> E[score E = sqrt of g squared plus dz tan e squared]
  E --> T[rank by E, ties: lower emission, fewer saturated, more coverage]
  K --> T2[rank backups by E after the natives]
  T --> V[convert the first in rank]
  T2 --> V
  V --> O[JP2_CONVERTED/*.png or *.jpg and ORTHO_SELECTION.csv]
    E = \sqrt{g^{2} + \left(\Delta z\,\tan e\right)^{2}},\qquad \text{ortho}^{*} = \arg\min E
    c = \frac{\#\{\text{valid DTM posts where the ortho has data}\}}{\#\{\text{valid DTM posts}\}},\qquad \text{backup if } c < c_{\max} - 0.01
    \text{reject} \iff f_0 = \frac{\#\{\mathrm{DN}=0 \lor \mathrm{DN}=\text{NoData}\}}{N} \ge 0.90 \;\;\lor\;\; \overline{\mathrm{DN}}_{(0\text{–}255)} < 2
    \begin{aligned} \ell &= \max\!\left(0,\; P_{2} - 0.05\,(P_{98}-P_{2})\right),\qquad h = \min\!\left(65535,\; P_{98} + 0.05\,(P_{98}-P_{2})\right)\\ \mathrm{DN}_8 &= \operatorname{clip}\!\left(255\,\frac{\mathrm{DN}-\ell}{h-\ell},\; 0,\; 255\right) \end{aligned}
    Sim. 3 · Stretch on a synthetic 16-bit ortho40,000 simulated pixels · percentiles computed live

    Zeros (instrument fill) are excluded before the percentiles, exactly as the converter does, so the black border around an ortho does not drag the stretch down.

    16-bit to 8-bit radiometric stretch

    3D engines need 8-bit textures. When the JP2 is not already 8-bit, the converter computes the 2nd and 98th percentiles of a ~512 px preview (ignoring zeros and NoData), pads the range by 5 % on each side, then maps it linearly to 0-255 with gdal.Translate(scaleParams=…).

    Fig. 7 · Stretch calculatorexample DN values

    Encoding. PNG is lossless on the native pixel grid. JPG uses quality 95, progressive, 4:4:4 chroma, and keeps the same grid unless one axis exceeds libjpeg's 65,500 px limit; then it decodes a smaller JPEG 2000 wavelet level (OVERVIEW_LEVEL) and Lanczos-resamples to fit. Results are cached in JP2_CONVERTED/.

    10 · Serialization

    3D formats and axes

    The mesh is built in the GIS convention: Z-up, X = east, Y = north, units in metres. Formats whose consumers expect Y-up get a remap on export: X stays, Y takes elevation, Z takes minus north. That keeps the coordinate system right-handed.

    Fig. 8 · Axis convention per formatexporters/*.py

    PLYbinary little-endianZvertex_indices listUVs as s,texport_ply
    FBXFBX 7.4 ASCIIYnative quadsmaterial referenceexport_fbx
    GLBglTF 2.0 binary: 12-byte header + JSON chunk + BIN chunkYtriangles, uint32 indicesembedded, PBR baseColorTextureexport_glb
    USDZuncompressed ZIP, 64-byte aligned, USDA root layerY, metersPerUnit = 1trianglesembedded, UsdPreviewSurfaceexport_usdz

    OBJ precision. Default "compact" writes vertices with 4 decimals and UVs with 6, without vn lines (importers rebuild normals from face winding). --full-precision switches to 9 decimals and --write-normals adds normals; the file grows about 3 to 4 times.

    \begin{pmatrix} x_g \\ y_g \\ z_g \end{pmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{R_x(-90^\circ)} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ z \\ -y \end{pmatrix},\qquad \det R = +1
    Fig. 8b · GLB byte layoutexporters/glb.py · every chunk padded to 4 bytes
    offset 0 "glTF" | version 2 | total length 12 B header [len][ "JSON" ] { accessors, bufferViews, materials, images } (space-padded) [len][ "BIN\0"] POSITION f32×3 · NORMAL f32×3 · TEXCOORD_0 f32×2 · indices u32×3 · image bytes

    Triangles ≈ 2 × quads ≈ 2N for a full grid, so indices take 3 × 4 × 2N bytes. Sizes are estimates from these formulas; the JSON chunk is a few kB.

    Fig. 8c · USDZ alignmentuncompressed ZIP, data aligned to 64 bytes

    Speed (v6.0.0)

    Writing millions of numbers as text was the slowest part of the run. np.savetxt called Python's % once per row; core/fastfmt.py now builds a million rows at a time with NumPy (four digits per table lookup into one character grid) and writes exactly what printf writes, so every mesh file is byte for byte the same as before. The five writers also run side by side (core/parallel.py, --jobs), and the point-cloud CSV is written in the background while the reports are built. Measured on a 2,500 × 5,000-post DTM, all formats, 2-core machine:

    PDF report images12 s< 1 s
    Whole run291 s≈ 30 s (9.8×)

    11 · Math modeling

    Science models

    Stage 6 attaches numbers to the terrain. They come in three kinds, and the report does not always say which is which, so this page labels them:

    measured computed from the DTM pixels   derived a formula applied to label, README or summary values   model a textbook curve drawn from a few summary numbers, not fitted to the DTM

    Stereo geometry and precision

    HiRISE DTMs come from two images of the same ground taken from different angles. The pipeline reads each image's emission angle θ (0° = straight down) from its PDS label and the bundle-adjustment residual (Total RMS, in pixels) from its README. The README RMS x, y and z are residuals of the tie to MOLA, not the DTM's precision.

    Fig. 9 · Stereo precision calculatorexample inputs · thresholds from science/kpis.py

    Grades follow the KPI thresholds: convergence good 15° to 30° (Sutton et al. 2022), warn 5° to 15° or 30° to 45°, critical below 5° (pipeline bands); EP good ≤ 1 m (a 1 m post), warn ≤ 2 m; Δa is the look-azimuth difference (from the PDS index since v6.3.9; without it the same-side value 0° is the worst case), 180° is opposite sides; Total RMS good < 0.5 px, acceptable ≤ 0.7 px (Sutton et al. 2022); PR = Total RMS / 0.2 px good ≤ 2.5, warn ≤ 3.5; relief / EP and ERI are pipeline metrics without grades. Surface pressure uses the exponential atmosphere p = 636 · e−h/11.0 km Pa (NASA NSSDCA Mars fact sheet) from mars_science.py, shown with its seasonal range (4.0 to 8.7 mbar at mean radius, scaled the same way).

    Typeset models

    \frac{B}{H} = \left\lvert \tan\theta_1\,\hat{u}(a_1) - \tan\theta_2\,\hat{u}(a_2) \right\rvert,\qquad \cos\gamma = \cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2 + \sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2\cos(a_1 - a_2)
    \lvert\tan\theta_1 - \tan\theta_2\rvert \le \frac{B}{H} \le \tan\theta_1 + \tan\theta_2,\qquad \lvert\theta_1 - \theta_2\rvert \le \gamma \le \theta_1 + \theta_2
    \mathrm{EP} = \frac{\rho\,\mathrm{GSD}}{B/H}\;(\rho = 0.2\ \mathrm{px}),\qquad \mathrm{PR} = \frac{\mathrm{RMS}_z}{\mathrm{EP}}
    \mathrm{RMS}_z = \sqrt{\mathrm{RMS}_{\text{tot}}^2 - \mathrm{RMS}_x^2 - \mathrm{RMS}_y^2},\quad \mathrm{SNR} = \frac{\Delta z}{\mathrm{RMS}_z},\quad \mathrm{DR} = 20\log_{10}\mathrm{SNR}\ \mathrm{dB},\quad b = \log_2 \mathrm{SNR},\quad \lambda_{\min} = 2\,\Delta\,s\ \ (\Delta = \text{DTM post spacing})
    \gamma_1 = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\tfrac{z-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^3\right],\quad \beta_2 = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\left(\tfrac{z-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^4\right],\quad \bar S = \arctan\sqrt{z_x^2 + z_y^2},\quad R = \frac{\Delta z}{\sqrt{W_{\text{ext}}^2 + H_{\text{ext}}^2}},\quad \mathrm{HI} = \frac{\bar z - z_{\min}}{\Delta z}
    \begin{aligned} p(z) &= \tfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(z-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}, & f(S) &= \tfrac{S}{\sigma_R^2}e^{-S^2/2\sigma_R^2},\ \sigma_R = \bar S\big/\sqrt{\pi/2}, & p_{\text{atm}}(h) &= 636\,e^{-h/11.1\,\mathrm{km}}\ \mathrm{Pa} \end{aligned}
    P(k) \propto k^{\beta}\ \ (\text{fit from 4 posts to tile}/4),\quad \gamma(h) = \tfrac12\,\overline{\left(z(x+h)-z(x)\right)^2},\quad \nu(\Delta x) = \sqrt{2\gamma(\Delta x)},\quad H = \frac{d\log\nu}{d\log\Delta x}
    s = \arctan\sqrt{\left(\frac{z_{c+k}-z_{c-k}}{2k\,\Delta x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{z_{r+k}-z_{r-k}}{2k\,\Delta y}\right)^2},\quad 2k\Delta x \in [2,5]\ \mathrm{m};\qquad r(L) = P_{99}\,\bigl\lvert z(\mathbf{x}+L) - z(\mathbf{x})\bigr\rvert,\quad L \le 1000\ \mathrm{m}
    Sim. 4 · Stereo viewing geometrywhy B/H from emission angles alone is an estimate

    MRO orbits at roughly 255-320 km. With looks on opposite sides of nadir the true convergence is θ₁ + θ₂; on the same side it is |θ₁ − θ₂|. Since v6.3.9 the sub-spacecraft points (SUB_SPACECRAFT_LATITUDE / LONGITUDE) and slant distances come from the PDS RDR cumulative index, so the true geometry is used for every archived image; only offline, without a local copy of the index, does the pipeline fall back to the range and the same-side lower bound.

    Fig. M3 · Model curves labMATLAB colour order · synthetic DTM for the measured panels
    measured on synthetic DTMtextbook curve (teaching only; the reports draw the measured curve, and label Gaussian and Rayleigh as models)
    Sim. 5 · Mars orbit and season (Ls)Kepler's equation · lbl_parser._classify_mars_season()
    M = \frac{2\pi t}{T},\quad M = E - e\sin E,\quad \tan\frac{\nu}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{1+e}{1-e}}\tan\frac{E}{2},\quad L_s = (\nu + 251.0^\circ) \bmod 360^\circ

    The pipeline reads Ls from each PDS label (SOLAR_LONGITUDE), checks it against this computation from START_TIME (v6.3.9), and names the northern season in 90° bins. This simulation shows where those numbers come from: perihelion falls at Ls ≈ 251°, so southern summer is short and hot and northern spring is the longest season.

    What changed in v6.3.9, and why

    The last estimates were replaced with archive data, and nine real PDS DTMs (82° N to 82° S) were checked against independent sources: 138 checks, 0 failed. A planetary scientist's review of a real north polar DTM (DTEPC_044810_2620) found 21 problems in the science text; all are fixed. The full list is in docs/HiRISE_v6.3.9_Scientific_Validation.html.

    What changed in v6.3.6, and why

    Every EDL grade now compares a measured number with a limit printed in a paper, and the two charts that showed fixed numbers now show measurements. Each row names its source.

    ChangeBefore (v6.3.5)After (v6.3.6)Source
    EDL slopeGraded from the relief ratio (relief over the footprint diagonal); quoted an MSL limit of 25° local, 5° regionalSlope measured at full resolution with a 2 to 5 m baseline, graded against 30°Golombek et al. 2012: slopes < 30° at baselines of 2 to 5 m
    Slope baselineLarge DTMs were read every k-th post, so the slope baseline could be tens of metresSmallest step with a 2 to 5 m baseline: 2 m at 1 m posts, 4 m at 2 m posts, 2 m at 0.5 m posts (step 2)Golombek et al. 2012; slopes depend on baseline (Kirk et al. 2008)
    EDL reliefNot measured; DATA/ said elevation span < 300 m preferred99th percentile of |z(x + L) − z(x)| at L = 10, 30, 100, 300 and 1000 m on a 10 m grid, graded against 100 to 130 mGolombek et al. 2012: relief < 100 to 130 m at baselines of 1 to 1000 m
    Elevation and latitudeElevation graded at ±1000 m around the areoid; DATA/ said < −500 m preferred; latitude not gradedMean elevation below −1 km and latitude within ±30° meet the MSL limitsGolombek et al. 2012
    Rock abundanceInferred from the valid fraction η, which measures stereo matching successNot assessed: rock abundance needs rock counts from imagesGolombek et al. 2012 lists it as its own constraint
    DTM resolutionGSD ≤ 1 m called sufficient for 10 m hazard detection, as an MSL standardPosts ≤ 2.5 m, so a two-post central difference spans 2 to 5 mFollows from the Golombek et al. 2012 baseline
    EDL chartFixed scores 20, 50, 20, 35, 40 for every DTMMeasured value ÷ MSL limit (100 % = at the limit)Golombek et al. 2012
    Mineral chartConfidence bars of 90, 85, 70 % and so on for every DTMPlain list labelled as a province rule table, with no confidence valueNo spectrometer data is read, so there is nothing to plot
    Slope distributionRayleigh curve drawn aloneMeasured histogram (2 to 5 m baseline) with the Rayleigh curve labelled model and fitted to the same dataRayleigh assumes independent Gaussian gradients; no Mars DTM paper adopts it
    Latitude zonesBoundaries at 15°, 30° and 60°Boundaries at 30° and 60° onlyMustard et al. 2001: ice-rich mantle at 30° to 60°
    Great-circle distancearccos form; points 1 cm apart gave 0Haversine form, full precision at every distanceGoldberg 1991; Snyder 1987
    Nyquist label2 × GSD × downsample, easily read as image GSD2 × post spacing × downsample, noted as a sampling limitKirk et al. 2020: DTMs resolve 10 to 20 image pixels
    Reference notesThe Golombek entry said 25 deg local / 5 deg regionalQuotes the abstract; four papers added, DOIs checked against CrossrefKirk et al. 2020, Mustard et al. 2001, Goldberg 1991, Snyder 1987

    Two grading rules are the pipeline's own, built on those limits: slope meets the limit when no post exceeds 30°, is a local exceedance when some do but P95 stays below 30°, and exceeds when P95 reaches 30°; relief uses the 99th percentile so one noisy post cannot fail a site. Both should be confirmed with Dr. Sutton.

    Every model, and how it is computed

    QuantityKindFormula / methodUnitCode

    Relief ratio RderivedΔz / √(W_ext² + H_ext²)dimensionlesskpis.py

    Nyquist wavelengthderivedλ_min = 2 · post spacing · downsample; a sampling limit, since stereo DTMs resolve 10 to 20 image pixels (measured on CTX and HRSC with HiRISE as the reference, Kirk et al. 2021; Sutton et al. 2022)mmars_science.py

    Reading notesfound while documenting the code
    • Archive data and the geologic map (fixed in v6.3.9). Stereo geometry and image pixel size come from the PDS RDR index, the unit and its age from the SIM 3292 polygons, and the science text follows the unit and the season (no basalt or summer CO2 frost on an ice cap); see What changed in v6.3.9.
    • Ground metres and real-data checks (fixed in v6.3.8). HiRISE map metres equal ground metres only at the projection’s centre latitude; slopes, areas and roughness now divide by the scale factor k = cos φ₁ / cos φ (Snyder 1987). Completeness is the fill inside the data footprint, since a complete HiRISE strip fills only about 75 % of its rectangle.
    • Precision and sources (fixed in v6.3.7). README RMS z is the residual of the tie to MOLA, not the precision; EP is now the precision everywhere, and every threshold either cites a source that states it or is labelled a pipeline choice; see What changed in v6.3.7.
    • EDL limits from the paper (fixed in v6.3.6). Slope and rock grades came from the relief ratio and the valid fraction, the Golombek et al. (2012) note quoted limits the paper does not state, and two report charts plotted fixed numbers. Slope and relief are now measured at the paper's baselines and graded against its limits; see What changed in v6.3.6.
    • Site location (fixed in v5.9.0). Geology, latitude zone, NPLD checks, the globe and the report metadata used the projection's central meridian and latitude of origin as the site; every polar DTM was placed at 90° N. One accessor, core/site.py, now returns the GDAL/OSR centre.
    • No stand-in numbers (fixed in v5.9.0). A chart whose input is missing (an LBL angle, README RMS, MAP_SCALE) is replaced by a "not drawn" card that names the missing input.
    • Measured statistics (fixed in v5.9.0). Spectrum slope, semivariogram, roughness, Hurst exponent, curvature, skewness, IQR, histogram, hypsometric curve and cross-section are measured from the DTM, not drawn from formulas or project-name lookups. Roughness classes no longer use RMS_z, which is the DTM's error, not its roughness.
    • Independent review, two rounds (v5.9.0). A second reviewer tried to break the math with rotated, mirrored and south-up rasters, the ±180° seam, poles, odd tile sizes, NoData holes and degenerate angles. Round 1 found 8 defects (GLB texture upside down, inside-out faces on south-up rasters, rotated pixel spacing, overhead-sun geometry, EP using the DTM post instead of the image GSD, seam/pole bounding box, rotated footprint, edge slopes). Round 2 found 9 more (odd-size spectrum crash, Laplacian on non-square posts, hole filling biasing β, label numbers like 2.5E-01, four leftover stand-in values, NaN lags, mirrored profile direction, site fallback order). All are fixed and each is a test.
    • B/H geometry (fixed in v5.8.4). Convergence used |θ₁ − θ₂| only. It now uses the look azimuths when the labels carry the sub-spacecraft point, and otherwise reports the range |tan θ₁ − tan θ₂| to tan θ₁ + tan θ₂ and grades with the lower bound.
    • Two EP values (fixed in v5.8.4). KPI tables used GSD / (B/H) while the 3D section used 0.2 GSD / (B/H). Every page now calls one function and uses Kirk et al. (2008), EP = 0.2 px × GSD / (B/H); the 1-pixel value is shown separately and labelled.
    • Slope spacing (fixed in v5.8.4). np.gradient now receives the true ground spacing; a 10 % test plane gives 5.71° at 0.5 m and 2 m posts.
    • Hypsometric integral (fixed in v5.8.4). The HTML page now uses (mean − min)/Δz from the real mean elevation, the same as the PDF and DATA/.
    • RMS_z labelled as EP (fixed in v5.8.4). Two report captions printed the README RMS_z under the name EP. They now say RMS_z, or EP only when RMS_z is missing.
    • Point-cloud lon/lat (fixed in v5.8.3). MESH_VERTICES.csv used to pass a CRS name where WKT is expected and fall back to an equirectangular inverse. It now transforms pixel centres through OSR in the DTM's own CRS, on exactly the mesh's vertices.
    • DATA/ centre and fill-ins (fixed in v5.8.3). DTM_KPI G04/G05 showed the projection's central meridian and latitude of origin as the site location, and missing RMS, B/H and emission angles were replaced by invented defaults. Both are gone; see How DATA/ stays connected.

    KPI scorecard

    science/kpis.py grades 50 KPIs, five in each of ten groups: terrain morphology, spatial resolution, raster quality, projection integrity, stereo geometry, mesh structure, reconstruction efficiency, observation context, photogrammetric accuracy, scientific usability. Each KPI has an ID (for example SU-04 EP = GSD/tan(Δθ)), a formula string, a unit and a good / warn / poor status from fixed thresholds.

    12 · Optional outputs

    Reports and data tables

    The report is where the back end hands off to a browser. Python does all the computation at build time and writes the results into the HTML as JavaScript arrays; when someone opens the file, CDN libraries draw the charts from those arrays. There is no server: the HTML file is the whole application.

    Optional outputs (v6.1.0). The 3D meshes are always written. The technical reports (Report/) and the data tables (DATA/) are each your choice: --reports yes|no and --data yes|no, short forms --no-reports and --no-data, or step 5 of the RUN.bat wizard. Leaving a flag out means yes. Try the four combinations below.

    15 · MATLAB
    
  
    MATLAB reproduction script
    
  
    A single MATLAB script that reproduces the core of the pipeline for one DTM: read, mask, downsample, mesh, normals, statistics, stereo precision and an OBJ + MTL export with the same layout. It uses base MATLAB plus readgeoraster / intrinsicToWorld from the Mapping Toolbox. It is a teaching and cross-checking tool; the Python pipeline remains the production path.
    
  
    
    
    hirise_mesh_demo.m
    

    %% hirise_mesh_demo.m
% Reproduces obj_pipeline Stage 1-5 core math for one HiRISE DTM.
% Author: Raymundo "R@y" Olguin, HiROC / LPL / University of Arizona
% Requires: MATLAB R2021a+ and Mapping Toolbox (readgeoraster, intrinsicToWorld)

dtmFile = 'DTEEC_082989_1630_083055_1630_A01.TIF';   % edit
texName = 'DTEEC_082989_1630_083055_1630_A01_Texture01.png';
stem    = erase(dtmFile, '.TIF');
B       = 1e7;        % --tri-budget (triangles)
kVE     = 1.0;        % vertical exaggeration (1 = none)

%% Stage 1: raster intake (NoData -> NaN)
[Z, R] = readgeoraster(dtmFile, 'OutputType', 'double');
info   = georasterinfo(dtmFile);
if ~isempty(info.MissingDataIndicator)
    Z(Z == info.MissingDataIndicator) = NaN;
end
Z(abs(Z) > 1e30) = NaN;
[H, W] = size(Z);

%% Stage 2: elevation screening
zv    = Z(isfinite(Z));
eta   = numel(zv) / numel(Z);                 % valid fraction
zmin  = min(zv);  zmax = max(zv);  dz = zmax - zmin;
mu    = mean(zv); sig  = std(zv, 1);          % population std, like np.nanstd
skew  = mean(((zv - mu) / sig).^3);
kurt  = mean(((zv - mu) / sig).^4);           % Pearson, normal = 3
HI    = (mu - zmin) / dz;                     % hypsometric integral
fprintf('valid %.4f  z %.2f..%.2f m  span %.2f m  HI %.3f\n', eta, zmin, zmax, dz, HI);

%% Stage 3: downsample, grid, vertices, UVs
Tfull = 2*(H-1)*(W-1);
if Tfull <= B, s = 1; else, s = ceil(sqrt(Tfull/B)); end
rows = 1:s:H; if rows(end) ~= H, rows(end+1) = H; end
cols = 1:s:W; if cols(end) ~= W, cols(end+1) = W; end
z     = Z(rows, cols);
valid = isfinite(z);
[C, Rr] = meshgrid(cols, rows);
[x, y]  = intrinsicToWorld(R, C, Rr);         % pixel centres (m)
idx = zeros(size(z)); idx(valid) = 1:nnz(valid);
V  = [x(valid), y(valid), kVE*z(valid)];
V(:,1:2) = V(:,1:2) - (min(V(:,1:2)) + max(V(:,1:2)))/2;   % centre XY
[oc, orr] = worldToIntrinsic(Ro, x, y);         % Ro = ortho raster reference
UV = [(oc(valid)-0.5)/Wo, 1 - (orr(valid)-0.5)/Ho];

%% Quads (a,b,c,d) and triangles (a,b,c)+(a,c,d)
a = idx(1:end-1,1:end-1); b = idx(2:end,1:end-1);
c = idx(2:end,2:end);     d = idx(1:end-1,2:end);
k = a>0 & b>0 & c>0 & d>0;
Q = [a(k) b(k) c(k) d(k)];
T = [Q(:,[1 2 3]); Q(:,[1 3 4])];
fprintf('downsample %d  vertices %d  triangles %d  retention %.3f%%\n', ...
        s, size(V,1), size(T,1), 100*size(T,1)/Tfull);

%% Area-weighted vertex normals (np.bincount equivalent: accumarray)
Fn = cross(V(T(:,2),:) - V(T(:,1),:), V(T(:,3),:) - V(T(:,1),:), 2);
N  = zeros(size(V));
for j = 1:3
    N(:,j) = accumarray(T(:), repmat(Fn(:,j), 3, 1), [size(V,1) 1]);
end
N = N ./ max(vecnorm(N, 2, 2), eps);
if mean(N(:,3)) < 0, N = -N; end

%% Stage 5: OBJ + MTL (compact: 4-decimal vertices, 6-decimal UVs, no vn)
fid = fopen([stem '_Material_01.mtl'], 'w');
mat = [stem '_Material_01'];
fprintf(fid, 'newmtl %s\nNs 10.0000\nKa 1.0000 1.0000 1.0000\nKd 1.0000 1.0000 1.0000\n', mat);
fprintf(fid, 'Ks 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000\nd 1.0\nillum 2\nmap_Kd %s\n', texName);
fclose(fid);
fid = fopen([stem '_Mesh01.obj'], 'w');
fprintf(fid, '# Terrain mesh: %s\n# Origin shifted to centroid\n', stem);
fprintf(fid, 'mtllib %s.mtl\no %s\nusemtl %s\n', mat, stem, mat);
fprintf(fid, 'v %.4f %.4f %.4f\n', V.');
fprintf(fid, 'vt %.6f %.6f\n', UV.');
fprintf(fid, 'f %d/%d %d/%d %d/%d %d/%d\n', Q(:,[1 1 2 2 3 3 4 4]).');
fclose(fid);

%% Stage 6 (excerpt): stereo precision from two label emission angles
th1 = 2.1; th2 = 19.6;                        % EMISSION_ANGLE from the two .LBL files (deg)
gsd = sqrt(R.CellExtentInWorldX * R.CellExtentInWorldY);
da  = 0;                                      % look azimuth difference (deg); 0 = same side (lower bound)
BH  = sqrt(tand(th1)^2 + tand(th2)^2 - 2*tand(th1)*tand(th2)*cosd(da));
gam = acosd(cosd(th1)*cosd(th2) + sind(th1)*sind(th2)*cosd(da));
EP  = 0.2 * gsd / BH;                         % Kirk et al. 2008, rho = 0.2 px (stereo_geometry.py)
fprintf('gamma %.2f deg  B/H %.4f  EP %.3f m\n', gam, BH, EP);

%% Quick look
figure; trisurf(T, V(:,1), V(:,2), V(:,3), 'EdgeColor', 'none');
axis equal tight; camlight headlight; lighting gouraud; colormap(parula); colorbar
xlabel('Easting (m)'); ylabel('Northing (m)'); zlabel('Elevation (m)');
title(strrep(stem, '_', '\_'));

    Output tree per project
    
  
    Everything the pipeline writes goes inside the project folder, next to the files it read; the only file outside is the run log in the --input folder. File names start with the DTM product ID (<id>, for example DTEEC_082989_1630_083055_1630_A01), so outputs from many projects never collide. A second run stops at existing outputs unless you pass --overwrite. Click a folder to open or close it; sizes are from the benchmark run (12.5 M posts, downsample 2, 3.1 M vertices, all formats, PNG ortho).
    
  
    input, read onlyalwaysif format chosen--reports yes--data yes
    
  
    
    
    <project>/input, read only53 MBThe project folder you point --input at (or one folder inside it). The pipeline only reads these files and never changes them.
      
    <id>.TIF | <id>.IMGinput, read only50 MBThe DTM: 32-bit elevations in metres, GeoTransform and projection. GeoTIFF or PDS3 IMG.
    
      
    *_RED_*_ORTHO.JP2input, read only3.1 MBOrthorectified images in JPEG 2000. One RED ortho becomes the texture, chosen by the scientific method (native grid, DTM coverage, lowest score E); IRB colour is never used.
    
      
    EXTRAS/*.LBLinput, read only2 × 1 kBPDS labels of the two source images: incidence, emission and phase angles, sun azimuth, MAP_SCALE, sub-spacecraft point, acquisition time.
    
      
    README.txtinput, read only< 1 kBThe DTM README: vertical RMS error, post spacing, producer notes. Missing values stay N/A.
    
    
    
    
    GeoTIF/if the DTM is a .IMG≈ DTM sizeThe GeoTIFF of every DTM .IMG (stage 0). Same elevations, georeferencing and NoData as the .IMG; the pipeline reads the DTM from here.
      
    <id>.TIFif the DTM is a .IMG≈ DTM sizeTiled, DEFLATE, predictor 3, BigTIFF; named exactly like the .IMG. Never rewritten unless --geotiff-overwrite.
    
    
    
    
    MESH/always1.6 GBThe 3D meshes, in projected map metres (east-west ground scale factor k in DATA), vertical exaggeration 1.0, origin at the centre of the mesh so engines do not lose float precision.
      
    <id>_Mesh01.obj--formats obj365 MBWavefront OBJ (text). Vertices to 4 decimals and UVs to 6 (9 with --full-precision), Z-up, X east, Y north. Opens in Blender, MeshLab, Maya, 3ds Max, Rhino.
    
      
    <id>_Material_01.mtl--formats obj205 BThe OBJ's material. Its map_Kd line names the texture next to it.
    
      
    <id>_Texture01.png|jpg--formats obj12.5 MBThe ortho texture, copied next to the OBJ so the OBJ, MTL, texture chain works when the folder is moved as a whole.
    
      
    <id>_TEXTURE_LINK.txt--formats obj2 kBPlain-text manifest: which MTL and texture the OBJ uses, whether each link was verified, and what to check if the mesh shows up white.
    
      
    <id>_Mesh01.ply--formats ply144 MBBinary PLY with positions and UVs (and normals with --write-normals), Z-up. For CloudCompare, MeshLab, Open3D.
    
      
    <id>_Mesh01.fbx--formats fbx540 MBASCII FBX 7.4, Y-up, texture referenced by file name. For Unity, Unreal, Maya, Twinmotion.
    
      
    <id>_Mesh01.glb--formats glb150 MBBinary glTF 2.0 with the texture embedded, Y-up. One file: drag into Twinmotion, Unreal, Blender, three.js or Babylon.js and it is already textured.
    
      
    <id>_Mesh01.usdz--formats usdz393 MBUSDZ with the full-resolution texture embedded (uncompressed, 64-byte aligned), Y-up. Opens in Apple Vision Pro, iPhone and iPad Quick Look, Reality Composer Pro.
    
    
    
    
    JP2_CONVERTED/always12.5 MBThe chosen ortho converted from JPEG 2000 to PNG or JPG, because most 3D tools cannot read JP2.
      
    <ortho>.png|jpgalways12.5 MB8-bit image with a percentile stretch. PNG is lossless; JPG (--ortho-format jpg) is about 10 times smaller.
    
      
    <ortho>.png.aux.xmlalways< 1 kBGDAL sidecar that keeps the georeferencing, so QGIS or ArcGIS place the image correctly on Mars.
    
      
    ORTHO_SELECTION.csvalways< 2 kBEvery ortho candidate with its grid, binning, emission, DTM coverage, score E and the decision in words: the record of why this texture was chosen.
    
    
    
    
    Twinmotion/alwaysemptyCreated empty for your own Twinmotion scenes and exports; the pipeline writes nothing here.
    
    
    
    Report/--reports yes3.9 MBThe three technical reports (see Reports and data tables).
      
    <id>_Technical_Report01.html--reports yes3.2 MBInteractive report with charts and 3D views. Keep it inside the project folder: it links to ../MESH/ and ../EXTRAS/.
    
      
    <id>_Technical_Report02.pdf--reports yes0.6 MBAbout 20 A4 pages for printing and e-mail.
    
      
    <id>_Technical_Report03.tex--reports yes41 kBLaTeX source for papers and theses; compile with pdflatex.
    
    
    
    
    DATA/--data yes335 MBExcel workbooks and CSV files (see Reports and data tables for every workbook and column).
      
    BY_PLANETARY_SCIENTIST/--data yes130 kB12 workbooks in three folders (SARAH_SUTTON, MATTHEW_CHOJNACKI, RAY_OLGUIN), each grouped for one line of research.
    
      
    PLANETARY_DATA/--data yes100 kB10 workbooks in four folders: PLANETARY_GEOLOGY, PLANETARY_SCIENCE, PROJECT_DATA, GIS_DATA.
    
      
    POINTCLOUD/MESH_VERTICES.csv--data yes334 MBOne row per mesh vertex: longitude, latitude, elevation, map and mesh coordinates.
    
      
    POINTCLOUD/MESH_VERTICES.xlsx--data yes0.6 MBThe first 10,000 vertices plus statistics and charts (Excel's row limit is 1,048,576).
    
      
    POINTCLOUD/DTM_KPI.csv  +  .xlsx--data yes5 kB + 33 kB71 key performance indicators in six groups, each with formula, value, unit and PASS / WARN / INFO.
    
    
    
    
    <input>/pipeline_errors_<date>_<time>.logalways2 to 5 kBOne run log per run, in the --input folder (outside the projects): start time, input root, then every warning and error as time, level, project, stage and message. WARN means the run continued; ERROR means a stage wrote nothing.
    
  
    
  
    Which file to open for what
    
  
    
    
    You want toOpen
    
    
      
    Edit or render the terrain in Blender, Maya, 3ds MaxMESH/<id>_Mesh01.obj (keep the MTL and texture beside it) or the GLB
    
      
    Build a scene in Twinmotion, Unreal or UnityMESH/<id>_Mesh01.glb (texture inside) or the FBX
    
      
    View it on Apple Vision Pro, iPhone or iPadMESH/<id>_Mesh01.usdz through the Files app
    
      
    Measure points, compare surfaces, clean the meshMESH/<id>_Mesh01.ply in CloudCompare or MeshLab
    
      
    Put the image on a map in QGIS or ArcGISJP2_CONVERTED/<ortho>.png (with its .aux.xml) next to the DTM
    
      
    Read the science summary or send it to someoneReport/<id>_Technical_Report01.html or the PDF
    
      
    Analyse the numbers in Excel, Python or MATLABDATA/ workbooks, DATA/POINTCLOUD/*.csv
    
      
    Find out why a run warned or a mesh is whiteThe run log, then MESH/<id>_TEXTURE_LINK.txt
